editorial:
The Patriot (1928) was Ernst Lubitsch's last silent-era Paramount production and one of the most celebrated lost films in Hollywood history. Emil Jannings plays the erratic Tsar Paul I of Russia; Lewis Stone is Count Pahlen, the loyalist officer who ultimately orchestrates the Tsar's assassination. The film was Paramount Famous Lasky Corp.'s first feature with spoken dialogue â€” a part-talkie with synchronized score and select sound sequences recorded in 1928. Hanns KrÃ¤ly won the Academy Award for Best Writing (Adaptation) for a screenplay drawn from Ashley Dukes's 1928 Broadway play, which itself adapted Alfred Neumann's 1925 German novel 'Der Patriot.' Five Academy Award nominations followed, including Best Picture â€” making this the only Best Picture nominee for which no complete or near-complete copy has ever been found. Roughly 2,500 feet of the original 10,000-foot print survive at the UCLA Film and Television Archive, with one additional reel recovered in Portugal.

For creators, the underlying copyright on every surviving frame is fully cleared: all US works published in 1928 entered the public domain on January 1, 2024 under the 95-year rule, and no renewal search is required. The one live trap is the score. The original 1928 synchronized soundtrack shares the film's PD status, but any musical score or sound design layered onto the surviving fragments by archivists or distributors after 1928 is separately protected from the date of that work. The trailer on Internet Archive (identifier: ThePatriotTrailer) is the most freely accessible moving-image remnant; use of UCLA's archival holdings requires the archive's permission as an access matter, not a copyright one.
faq: Is The Patriot (1928) in the public domain?

Yes, unconditionally. US copyright law draws a bright line at 1930: every American film published that year or earlier is public domain in full. The Patriot was released by Paramount in 1928, so its 95-year copyright term expired on January 1, 2024. Renewal status is irrelevant â€” even a timely-renewed 1928 film reached the end of its maximum 95-year term on that date.
Can I use the surviving trailer and fragments from Archive.org freely?

The underlying footage is PD â€” the copyright cleared January 1, 2024. The practical check is the sound layer: if the copy you are using carries a modern musical score or sound effects added after 1928, that audio is separately protected from the year of its creation. The Archive.org trailer (identifier: ThePatriotTrailer) preserves material sourced from Paramount's 1928 campaign. For fragments held by UCLA, clearance is an archival-access question for the institution, not a copyright question.
